name: Truth Mirror
oneLiner: A lightweight, transparent pipeline that verifies geopolitical claims by retrieving global sources, analyzing media blocs, and synthesizing a structured verdict with confidence and provenance.
tech: RSS & news connectors (Google News RSS, GDELT)
Web scraping & parsing (feedparser, beautifulsoup4, requests, aiohttp)
problem: Consumers and analysts lack a fast, auditable way to evaluate complex geopolitical claims across diverse global sources; existing tools either give simple binary answers or obscure which sources and reasoning produced them. This makes it hard to detect narrative divergence, media-bloc framing, or partially supported assertions.
approach: Truth Mirror implements a modular multi-step pipeline that routes work to specialized components and multiple model providers. Incoming text passes a scope gate to detect geopolitical claims, then a decomposition step breaks the claim into verifiable sub-claims. A retrieval orchestrator queries parallel connectors (Wikipedia/Wikinews, Google News RSS, GDELT, Semantic Scholar, arXiv, PubMed, fact-check feeds and others) with configurable ordering (news-first for current/political claims). Retrieved items are normalized into EvidenceItem records, de-duplicated, scored for relevance/credibility, and grouped by perspective. Short, fast classification and extraction tasks are routed to Groq; deeper synthesis and structured JSON verdict generation use Google Gemini with a key-rotator and a tertiary OpenRouter fallback. The pipeline applies temporal validation, stance analysis, hostile-source triangulation and narrative clustering to surface both consensus and disputed points. Results and intermediate run metadata are cached in a local SQLite store (WAL), logged to a testing log, and emitted as a consistent JSON schema consumed by a lightweight HTML/JS dashboard. Engineering safeguards include rate-limit mini-batching, a 5-minute execution timeout, JSON-repair/fence-stripping for noisy LLM outputs, and basic HTTP auth for the UI.
outcome: Users receive a structured intelligence report instead of a single label: a final verdict with confidence scores, evidence summaries, key sources, media-bloc perspective cards, a breakdown of what is supported/contradicted/unclear, and flagged 'hidden stories' or omissions. The system is modular and runnable locally (or via the provided docker-compose), with caching to reduce repeated API costs and a fallback model route to improve availability. Notable strengths are the explicit source provenance, multi-provider routing, and news-first retrieval logic for geopolitical claims. Practical limitations include dependency on external (often paid) LLM APIs and variable latency (analysis can take minutes), plus sensitivity to retrieval quality (good sources matter more than model size). Clear next improvements include adding an async job queue / worker architecture for long-running analyses, a human-review workflow and audit trail UI, expanded connector coverage and automated tests. The key tradeoff learned here is that reliable retrieval and properly-scoped evidence handling drive trustworthy verdicts more than raw model capacity.

name: Fake Forward App
oneLiner: An automated fact-checking web app that extracts checkable claims from forwarded messages, retrieves evidence from Wikipedia and DuckDuckGo, and returns per-claim scores and a final verdict to help users debunk viral forwards quickly. (Built for the National AI Hackathon'26)
problem: People frequently receive long, emoji-filled forwarded messages (WhatsApp, Telegram, social media) that bundle multiple factual claims; manually verifying each claim is slow and error-prone, so misinformation spreads rapidly in group chats and casual conversations.
approach: The app runs a linear, four-stage pipeline served by a FastAPI backend and a zero-dependency frontend. First an LLM-based extractor parses pasted text and returns up to five objective, checkable claims. The searcher concurrently queries the Wikipedia REST API and DuckDuckGo (via the duckduckgo-search package) to gather evidence. The scorer feeds the claim plus retrieved evidence back to an LLM to produce a numeric score (0-100), a short evidence summary, and a preliminary verdict; if no search hits are found the scorer can rely on the model's internal knowledge to avoid wasted API calls. A verdict module aggregates per-claim scores into an overall verdict and mapped category. Engineering choices for reliability include strict HTTP and LLM timeouts, a JSON-repair pass for malformed LLM outputs, an LLM fallback to a local model (Ollama/qwen2.5), bounded input sizes, brief sleeps to mitigate provider rate limits, and robust exception handling so the API degrades gracefully. The frontend is static HTML/CSS/vanilla JS (GPU-accelerated visuals, accessibility-respecting animations) mounted directly by FastAPI.
outcome: Users get a fast, shareable fact-check: individual claim scores, color-coded verdicts (TRUE / PROBABLE / FALSE / UNVERIFIABLE), short evidence summaries, and a one-click copyable report to paste into chats. The app is lightweight, local-deployable, and tuned for hackathon-grade resilience (timeouts, fallbacks, JSON repair). Key limitations are typical of retrieval+LLM systems: results depend heavily on the quality and recency of retrieved sources and on model knowledge; edge cases can produce uncertain or incorrect scores. Natural next improvements are adding provenance links and source-weighting, caching and rate-limit-aware batching, richer multi-source triangulation, and a more explicit trust/scoring rubric — the main lesson here is that careful retrieval, timeouts, and fallback logic materially improve practical reliability more than pushing model size alone.

name: Meow Or Woof
oneLiner: A lightweight PyTorch transfer-learning classifier with a Gradio web UI that predicts whether an uploaded image contains a cat or a dog.
problem: Developers, students, and hobbyists need a simple, reproducible example to build and test an image classification pipeline — including training, checkpointing, and an interactive UI — without wiring up a full ML infra or dataset preprocessing flow
approach: The project uses transfer learning with a torchvision EfficientNet-B0 backbone preloaded with ImageNet weights. A custom Dataset parses labels from flat filenames (cat* -> 0, dog* -> 1) and train/validation splits are produced with sklearn (80/20). Training applies basic augmentations (RandomHorizontalFlip, RandomRotation, ColorJitter) and normalizes inputs to the ImageNet statistics. The base EfficientNet parameters are frozen; only a replaced linear classifier head is trained with Adam and CrossEntropyLoss for a small number of epochs (default 5). The best checkpoint (by validation accuracy) is saved to model/meow_or_woof.pth and training curves are emitted as a PNG. For inference a small Gradio Blocks app loads the same EfficientNet architecture, restores the saved weights, runs the image through standard resize/normalize transforms, applies softmax to model logits, and shows class confidence bars. The code includes a DEBUG_MODE to subset data for quick tests and selects DEVICE automatically (CUDA if available).
outcome: A runnable, end-to-end prototype that trains a two-class cat vs. dog classifier and exposes it via an interactive Gradio UI for instant image-level predictions with confidence scores. It's a compact, reproducible baseline useful for demos, learning, and quick experimentation; training is fast because the backbone is frozen and only the head is optimized. Limitations include the absent dataset in the repo (Kaggle download required), a short default training schedule and no held-out test split, and limited preprocessing or class-balance handling. Natural next steps are longer training, selective fine-tuning of late backbone layers, improved augmentations and calibration, and packaging the app for remote serving. The main lesson here is that transfer learning yields a practical, low-cost baseline quickly — but final accuracy depends more on dataset quality and augmentation than on brute model size.

name: Digit Recognition — MNIST
oneLiner: A compact, end-to-end TensorFlow/Keras pipeline that trains a CNN on MNIST to classify handwritten digits and exports a ready-to-use .keras model.
problem: Learners and practitioners often need a reproducible, easy-to-run example that demonstrates the full lifecycle of training a convolutional neural network (preprocessing → augmentation → training → evaluation → export) for handwritten digit classification. Without a concise reference, it's hard to see how model architecture, data pipeline, callbacks, and visualizations fit together into a runnable workflow.
approach: The repository implements a single-file, reproducible pipeline: it loads MNIST via Keras, normalizes and reshapes images to (28,28,1), and one-hot encodes labels. A light tf.data pipeline applies on-the-fly augmentation (random rotation, zoom, translation) and uses batching, shuffling and prefetching for throughput. The model is a compact CNN (three Conv2D + BatchNorm blocks, followed by a Dense(256) head and Dropout(0.4)). Training uses Adam, categorical cross-entropy, and practical callbacks (EarlyStopping restoring best weights and ReduceLROnPlateau). After training the code evaluates on the test set, produces per-class reports and a confusion matrix via scikit-learn, saves diagnostic plots (sample images, training curves, confusion matrix, prediction grid) and exports the trained model in Keras .keras format. Engineering choices focus on clarity and reproducibility: tf.data for performance, BatchNorm and Dropout for regularization, and small, interpretable architecture to reach high accuracy quickly.
outcome: The project yields a runnable example that typically reaches ~99% test accuracy on MNIST, produces visual artifacts (training curves, confusion matrix, sample predictions) and a saved .keras model ready for inference. It's a strong educational and baseline resource for experimenting with CNNs, augmentation and callback strategies. Areas for improvement include adding a CLI/inference API, unit tests, model versioning or quantization for deployment, and extending preprocessing for more realistic handwriting variations. The main lesson: lightweight, well-instrumented pipelines with modest architectures and targeted augmentation can achieve excellent accuracy quickly on benchmark datasets, but additional work is required to move from a clear demo to production-ready robustness.

name: NUSTcord
oneLiner: A self-hosted, Java Servlet + JSP Discord-style chat platform for university communities that demonstrates secure, layered OOP design and ships as a Tomcat-deployable WAR.
problem: Small organizations or campus communities need a lightweight, self-hosted group chat and community-management platform (servers, channels, DMs, friends) without relying on external services; additionally, the project addresses the educational need to demonstrate real-world OOP and MVC design without heavy frameworks.
approach: NUSTcord uses a strict MVC layering implemented with Java Servlets (controllers), a Service layer for business rules, DAOs for JDBC access, and JSP views for the UI. It persists data in an embedded H2 relational database (schema and seed data applied at startup by a ServletContextListener). Security is handled with jBCrypt for salted password hashing, session-based authentication guarded by an AuthFilter, and SQL queries executed with PreparedStatements to reduce injection risk. The system models servers, channels, roles, friend-requests, direct messages and message history as normalized tables (composite keys and ON DELETE CASCADE where appropriate). The app is built with Maven and packaged as a WAR for Tomcat; UI is vanilla JSP/HTML/CSS/JS with reusable JSP includes and a dark theme. Engineering choices emphasize clarity and pedagogy: explicit JDBC instead of an ORM, idempotent DB init, centralized password utility, and an AdminDAO that aggregates cross-table statistics for the admin dashboard.
outcome: The repository implements a fully functional prototype: user registration and secure login, online-status tracking, friend request lifecycle, server creation and membership/role management, per-server text channels, persistent direct messages, and an admin dashboard with live client-side search and sorting. It is easy to run locally (embedded H2 and seed accounts, WAR deploy to Tomcat) and serves both as a usable campus chat app prototype and a clear OOP/MVC teaching example. Notable limitations include the lack of real-time transport (no WebSocket/Push for live updates), an embedded single-file H2 database not suited for multi-node production, and hand-rolled session management that could be improved by a framework or centralized auth. The clearest lesson is that keeping layers explicit (Service → DAO → Model) and minimizing hidden framework magic makes both security and reasoning about behavior (like seeding, cascades, and auth) much easier for learning and small deployments.
